source: In the S bus, in the rush hour. A chap of about 26, felt hat with a cord instead of a ribbon, neck too long, as if someone’s been having a tug-of-war with it. People getting off. The chap in question gets annoyed with one of the men standing next to him. He accuses him of jostling him every time anyone goes past. A snivelling tone which is meant to be aggressive. When he sees a vacant seat he throws himself on to it. Two hours later, I meet him in the Cour de Rome, in front of the gare Saint-Lazare. He’s with a friend who’s saying: "You ought to get an extra button put on your overcoat." He shows him where (at the lapels) and why.
prompt:
You are assisting with a scholarly experiment in structural literary analysis.

TASK: Write an ORIGINAL short prose passage in English, set in the target scenario below. It must be
a HOMEOSYNTACTIC transposition of a hidden source: hold the source's syntactic form at the level
specified below while inventing entirely new words and moving the content into the target
scenario. It is NOT a paraphrase or a translation.

FORM TARGET (hold this). Reproduce, period by period, the CLAUSE ARCHITECTURE below --- the same inventory and nesting of clauses (main / relative / adverbial / complement / coordinate, to the stated depth). The WORD ORDER and the words themselves are entirely yours; only the clause skeleton is fixed.
Reproduce it for all 10 periods, in this order:
Period 1 (~8 words) clause architecture: 1 main clause; subordination nested up to depth 0.
Period 2 (~29 words) clause architecture: 1 main clause; 1 open complement (infinitive); 1 adverbial clause; subordination nested up to depth 1.
Period 3 (~3 words) clause architecture: 1 main clause; subordination nested up to depth 0.
Period 4 (~15 words) clause architecture: 1 main clause; 1 relative/adnominal clause; subordination nested up to depth 1.
Period 5 (~11 words) clause architecture: 1 main clause; 1 adverbial clause; 1 relative/adnominal clause; subordination nested up to depth 2.
Period 6 (~9 words) clause architecture: 1 main clause; 1 relative/adnominal clause; 1 open complement (infinitive); subordination nested up to depth 2.
Period 7 (~12 words) clause architecture: 1 adverbial clause; 1 main clause; subordination nested up to depth 1.
Period 8 (~18 words) clause architecture: 1 main clause; subordination nested up to depth 0.
Period 9 (~19 words) clause architecture: 2 relative/adnominal clause; 1 main clause; 1 finite complement clause; 1 open complement (infinitive); subordination nested up to depth 4.
Period 10 (~9 words) clause architecture: 1 main clause; 1 finite complement clause; subordination nested up to depth 1.

TARGET SCENARIO --- render the content here (in your own words):
  - a supermarket checkout line at a busy hour
  - the conveyor belt, the barcode scanner, the bagging area, the card reader
  - the cashier and a shopper; a cart, a divider bar, a receipt
  - another shopper crowding from behind; a small friction over space in the queue
  - the register of retail routine: beeps, the total announced, loyalty-card prompts

REQUIREMENTS --- both hold together:
1. CLAUSE ARCHITECTURE PRESERVED --- the same clause inventory and nesting depth per period, in any word order and words you choose.
2. COHERENT --- one continuous, fully sensible passage in the target scenario; new lexicon,
   no trace of any source content.

Write modern, natural English. Produce the 10 periods in order as continuous prose --- no
numbering, no headings. Output ONLY the passage: no preamble, no self-audit.

gens.text:
The line stretched toward the register.

She had been waiting to unload her cart onto the belt, though the woman ahead of her kept fumbling for coupons while the cashier stood idle, scanning nothing, tapping her nails against the counter.

The scanner beeped.

The barcode reader, which had misfired twice already, finally caught the label. Because the total climbed higher than she expected, the receipt that spooled out seemed absurdly long. The register demanded she swipe again, refusing to accept her chip. Whenever the belt lurched forward, the divider bar slid toward the bagging area. The man behind her crowded closer, edging his basket against her hip. He wanted his space and he took it, greedily, without a word.

The clerk asked whether I carried a loyalty card that entitled me to the discount she claimed the flyer had promised, though I could not remember to bring it. She announced that the card reader had finally approved my payment.

The line stretched past the magazine rack. She unloaded her cart onto the belt, pausing to steady a wobbling carton, while the scanner chirped its steady rhythm ahead. Beeps multiplied. The cashier, whose badge read Marta, dragged each item across the glowing red glass. Because the bagging area filled quickly, groceries slid against a wall that nobody had cleared. The woman behind pressed forward, eager to unload her basket. When the divider bar clattered down, the shopper reclaimed her narrow stretch of belt. The total appeared on the small screen with its glaring green digits and its cheerful little prompt about loyalty points. A man who tapped his card, whose patience had thinned, muttered that the machine, which kept declining, refused to admit the chip had failed. Marta smiled and said the receipt was printing.

The line coiled past the endcap displays. She wanted to unload her basket quickly, though the conveyor belt kept stalling under the weight of the shopper ahead. The scanner beeped. A cart nudged the divider bar that she had placed between their groceries. Because the aisle narrowed where the card reader sat, the man behind pressed closer than felt polite. The cashier paused to reprint a receipt that had jammed. When the loyalty prompt flashed, she fumbled for her phone. The bagging area filled with cans and cartons and bruising fruit. She sensed that the stranger crowding her elbow believed the queue that stretched behind him would somehow move faster if he leaned in to hurry her. The cashier announced that the total came to forty dollars.

The line stretched past the magazine rack. She unloaded her cart onto the belt, meaning to keep things orderly, though the man behind her had already pressed too close. The scanner beeped. The cashier, whose badge read Tuesday's trainee, swept each item toward the bagging area. When the divider bar slid forward, the groceries that belonged to the stranger nudged against her own. The total appeared, waiting for her to tap the reader. Because the machine paused, she frowned at the prompt. The loyalty screen asked whether she wanted points collected on a card she had forgotten to bring. The receipt, which curled from the slot and which nobody wanted, printed slowly while she realized that the man expected her to move faster. He muttered that the space was his too.

The line at register four was long. She unloaded her cart onto the belt, wanting to finish quickly, because the man behind her had already pressed his basket against the small plastic divider. The scanner beeped. The cashier, whose hands moved without any pause, dragged each item across the glass. Whenever a barcode failed, she keyed the numbers that glowed faintly on the label. The shopper leaned forward, eager to reach the card reader. As the total climbed higher, the bags filled steadily. The machine asked her whether she carried a loyalty card in her wallet. The man who edged closer, who clearly believed his time mattered more, sighed loudly and muttered that she ought to hurry along. She tapped her card and hoped the receipt would print.

The line stretched past the magazine racks.

To keep the queue moving, the cashier swept each item across the scanner, while a green light blinked and the register logged another price.

Groceries piled up.

A woman unloaded her cart onto the belt, which glided everything toward the bagging area.

Because she paused to fumble for coupons that the machine kept rejecting, the man behind sighed.

He edged his basket forward, wanting to claim the counter space.

When she set the divider bar between their orders, he frowned slightly.

The scanner beeped steadily through cans and boxes and the bright plastic bags rustling below the shelf.

The clerk, whose badge read a name nobody bothered to read, announced that the total had climbed higher than the shopper had expected to spend.

The card reader prompted that a loyalty number was still missing.

The line coiled toward the register at dusk. She began to unload her cart onto the conveyor belt, stacking cans in careful rows while the belt shuddered forward with a low hum. The scanner blinked. A woman ahead fumbled with coupons that had crumpled inside her purse. Because the bagging area was crowded, the sacks she filled slumped against a rail. The cashier reached for the divider bar to steady it. When another shopper pressed too near, the cart nudged her heels. The card reader chirped its impatient prompt for a signature. The man behind her, whose basket teetered against her spine, muttered that he hoped the clerk would hurry to finish scanning. The cashier announced that the total came to nothing much.

The line stretched past the frozen aisle. She unloaded her basket onto the belt, careful to nudge the divider forward before the man behind her could crowd the narrow gap. The scanner beeped. A jar of olives, which had rolled sideways near the register, refused to read on the first pass. When the cashier lifted it toward the light that hung above the terminal, the barcode finally caught. The shopper reached to steady the bag that threatened to tip. Because the belt kept advancing, she stacked the cans quickly. The card reader flashed its familiar prompt for a loyalty number and a signature. The man whose cart pressed against her heels muttered that the queue was slow, and she suspected he wanted her to hurry, though the total still climbed on the display. The cashier announced that the receipt was printing.

The line stretched past the magazine rack. She unloaded her cart onto the conveyor belt, wanting to finish before the lunch rush swelled, while the scanner beeped steadily at the next station over. The belt lurched. A divider bar, which someone had left askew, slid toward her groceries with a clatter. When the cashier waved her forward, the woman whose milk was leaking hurried too. She kept a receipt, which fluttered down, to prove the discount. Because the man behind pressed closer, her elbow bumped the card reader. He shoved his basket against the plastic edge, muttering something about people who dawdled and never learned to move along quickly. The cashier, who paused mid-scan, announced the total that the display had flashed, saying the loyalty prompt still needed her number to save. She realized then that the receipt held everything.

The line stretched past the magazine racks.

She unloaded her cart onto the belt with practiced haste, wanting to finish before the store filled completely, since the after-work crowd always surged through these doors at six.

The scanner beeped.

The cashier, whose hands moved with mechanical certainty, dragged each item across the glass. Because the belt kept advancing, the divider bar that separated the orders slid forward too. The woman behind her, who was eager to begin, edged her basket up to press. Already the receipt was printing, and the total glowed red.

While the card reader hummed, the shopper tapped her phone against it. She fumbled for the loyalty card that always hid in her wallet's deepest fold.

The stranger crowding from behind sighed loudly and shifted her weight and huffed at the delay.

The cashier, who noticed the tension building silently between the two women there, decided to speak up and asked them both to breathe.

They confirmed that everything was fine.
